sec.title: Background
sec.p: This first-in-human study evaluated EGFRvIII × CD3 TCB, a novel T cell bispecific antibody, in patients with newly diagnosed EGFRvIII-positive glioblastoma.

sec.title: Methods
sec.p: Patients with newly diagnosed glioblastoma received escalating doses of EGFRvIII × CD3 TCB following chemoradiation. The primary objectives were to evaluate safety/tolerability and define the maximum tolerated dose (MTD); secondary objectives included pharmacokinetics (PK), immunogenicity, pharmacodynamics, and clinical activity.

sec.title: Results
sec.p: Thirty-six patients were enrolled, 32 with unmethylated and 4 with methylated MGMT promoter. EGFRvIII × CD3 TCB doses ranged from 0.004 to 10 mg Q3W, administered either on a flat or step-up dose schedule. One DLT occurred (grade 3 seizure). The MTD was not reached. Most adverse events (AEs) were of grade 1-2 severity, with headache being the most common treatment-related AE (22%). EGFRvIII × CD3 TCB showed dose-proportional PK in serum and cerebrospinal fluid (CSF), with a CSF/serum ratio of 0.08. At the highest dose tested, 10 mg Q3W, maximum serum concentrations remained 6-fold below the lower boundary of the predicted anticipated therapeutic dose.

sec.title: Conclusions
sec.p: The administration of EGFRvIII × CD3 TCB in a maintenance setting, following standard of care treatment, was safe and well tolerated up to the highest tested dose of 10 mg Q3W. However, evidence of efficacy was not observed at the evaluated doses, suggesting that a study of higher dose levels may be warranted.

list-item.p: This was a first-in-human study of EGFRvIII × CD3 TCB, a T cell bispecific antibody, in newly EGFRvIII-positive glioblastoma.
The highest tested dose of 10 mg Q3W was very well tolerated. Testing of higher doses is warranted to evaluate antitumor efficacy further.

boxed-text.p: There is an urgent need for new GBM treatment approaches. This first-in-human study evaluated EGFRvIII × CD3 TCB, a novel T cell bispecific antibody, in patients with newly diagnosed EGFRvIII-positive glioblastoma. The administration of EGFRvIII × CD3 TCB in a maintenance setting, following standard of care treatment, was safe and well tolerated up to the highest tested dose of 10 mg Q3W. The phase 1 nature of the study and the fact that the highest dose tested was below the predicted anticipated therapeutic dose preclude conclusions on efficacy.

body.p: Glioblastoma (GBM) is the most common and aggressive primary brain tumor, accounting for approximately 50% of all malignant gliomas.1,2 For patients with newly diagnosed GBM, the standard treatment consists of surgery for tumor debulking, followed by concurrent chemoradiotherapy and adjuvant temozolomide. The median survival time with this regimen is 15 months, based on results from the EORTC-NCIC trial, with less than 10% of patients surviving for more than 5 years.3 Patients with tumors containing an unmethylated MGMT promoter, who account for up to 60% of all patients with GBM,4 have limited benefit from treatment with temozolomide and, therefore, a worse prognosis than patients with methylated MGMT promoter.5,6 This and the high probability of disease recurrence, for which there is no established standard of care,7 emphasize the high unmet medical need in GBM and an opportunity to test novel agents in the front-line setting.

Epidermal growth factor receptor variant III (EGFRvIII), an in-frame deletion of exons 2-7, is observed in about 20% of GBMs,8 and results in a constitutively active EGFR,9 which has been shown to enhance tumorigenicity,10 promote cellular motility,11 and confer resistance to radiation and chemotherapy.12 EGFRvIII is absent in normal tissues,13 making it a promising target for immunotherapies such as T cell bispecific (TCB) antibodies. Previous approaches targeting EGFR or EGFRvIII in newly diagnosed GBM have not demonstrated significantly improved outcomes for patients in clinical trials; these include the EGFRvIII peptide rindopepimut and anti-EGFR antibody nimotuzumab, both of which were added to standard therapy, and anti-EGFRvIII CAR T cells in combination with pembrolizumab.14–16 In recurrent GBM, the use of anti-EGFRvIII CAR T cells engineered to secrete T cell engaging antibody molecules (TEAMs) against wildtype EGFR showed encouraging results, but these still need to be confirmed in a larger number of patients.17

Bispecific antibodies, which can bridge immune cells with cancer cells by binding two different antigens, have received regulatory approval for the treatment of various hematological and certain solid tumors.18,19 EGFRvIII × CD3 TCB (RO7428731) is a novel TCB antibody that targets both human EGFRvIII expressed on GBM cells and cluster of differentiation (CD)3ε present on T cells.20 EGFRvIII × CD3 TCB binds in a bivalent binding mode with high avidity to human EGFRvIII, whereas the binding to CD3ε is monovalent. The two anti-EGFRvIII fragment antigen-binding (Fab) domains are selective for human EGFRvIII and do not bind to wild-type EGFR. EGFRvIII × CD3 TCB showed T cell activation and concomitant T cell-mediated killing of GBM cells in vitro and in vivo in xenograft orthotopic tumor models, including patient-derived tissue models, and was able to access the tumor in the brain.20

In this first-in-human study, we explored the use of EGFRvIII × CD3 TCB as monotherapy in patients with newly diagnosed EGFRvIII-positive GBM without progression after completion of chemoradiation (Supplementary Figure S1).

sec.title: Study Design
sec.p: This was an open-label, multicenter, first-in-human, phase 1 dose-escalation study. The primary objectives were to evaluate the safety and tolerability of EGFRvIII × CD3 TCB and determine the maximum tolerated dose (MTD). Secondary objectives included pharmacokinetics (PK), anti-EGFRvIII × CD3 TCB immune response, preliminary antitumor activity, and determination of the recommended dose for expansion (RDE)/recommended phase 2 dose (RP2D). Exploratory objectives included biomarkers and treatment-induced pharmacodynamic effects such as blood cytometry, cytokines as well as cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) analysis.

The study was conducted in accordance with the Declaration of Helsinki and the International Council for Harmonization of Technical Requirements for Pharmaceuticals for Human Use (ICH) Good Clinical Practice (GCP) Guidelines. The institutional review board of each study site approved the study. All enrolled patients provided written informed consent to participate. This study is registered with ClinicalTrials.gov (NCT05187624).

sec.title: Study Population
sec.p: Patients aged ≥ 18 years were eligible if they were newly diagnosed with GBM based on the WHO classification of CNS tumors, 5th edition (2021) and had confirmed EGFRvIII expression using an investigational EGFRvIII immunohistochemistry (IHC) assay (≥ 1% of tumor cell expression with ≥ 1 + staining intensity) in a CAP/CLIA-accredited central testing laboratory; a life expectancy of ≥ 12 weeks; Karnofsky Performance Status (KPS) score of ≥ 70; a corticosteroid dose ≤ 2 mg/day of dexamethasone (or equivalent dose of other corticosteroids) within 5 days prior to start of study treatment; and adequate organ functions within 7 days prior to start of study treatment. A complete list of eligibility criteria is included in the Supplementary Methods. MGMT promoter methylation analysis was performed locally according to institutional guidelines.

Patients with unmethylated MGMT promoter had to have completed standard of care therapy with surgical resection and adjuvant radiotherapy, with or without concomitant temozolomide, with or without any number of cycles of temozolomide maintenance as long as there was no evidence of tumor recurrence. Patients with methylated MGMT promoter had to have completed standard temozolomide chemoradiotherapy plus adjuvant temozolomide without tumor progression or had discontinued or declined adjuvant temozolomide for reasons other than progressive disease.

sec.title: Study Treatment
sec.p: Patients received study treatment for up to 1 year or until disease progression (unless the patient experienced clinical benefit per investigator judgment or confirmation of progression was pending), unacceptable toxicity, or withdrawal of consent. EGFRvIII × CD3 TCB was administered via an intravenous (IV) infusion, with corticosteroid premedication employed for the first 2 cycles of treatment. Flat doses of EGFRvIII × CD3 TCB were administered once every 3 weeks (Q3W) in the first 8 cohorts (Supplementary Figure S2). A step-up dosing (SUD) schedule was explored in two additional cohorts in which patients received an initial lower dose on day 1 of cycle 1 followed by a higher target dose on day 8 of cycle 1, and then Q3W as a flat dose from cycle 2 onwards. Each cycle of study therapy was 21 days. Tocilizumab was allowed for the treatment of cytokine-release syndrome (CRS).

sec.title: Dose Escalation
sec.p: The EGFRvIII × CD3 TCB starting dose of 0.004 mg was determined using an in vitro minimal anticipated biological effect level (MABEL) approach and corresponded to a concentration of EGFRvIII × CD3 TCB at which 30% pharmacological activity of tumor cell killing was observed in a 3D blood–brain-barrier-GBM model with a high EGFRvIII-expressing cell line. The pharmacological minimally active dose (mPAD) of EGFRvIII × CD3 TCB was anticipated to be approximately 0.4 mg Q3W. The anticipated therapeutic dose (ATD) in humans resulting in plasma exposures between 8.8 and 20 μg/mL was anticipated to be in the range of 80 to 330 mg Q3W based on allometric scaling from hFcRn Tg32 mice (transgenic mice expressing human neonatal Fc receptor). Dose escalation was guided by a modified Continual Reassessment Method with an Escalation with Overdose Control (mCRM with EWOC). Dose-limiting toxicity (DLT) criteria included significant and related adverse events (AEs) during cycle one, and are specified in the Supplementary Methods. A new dose cohort could only be opened after at least three patients in the previous cohort completed the DLT observation period of 21 days, starting from the first infusion of EGFRvIII × CD3 TCB.

Intra-patient dose escalation up to doses that did not surpass the MTD was allowed starting from cycle 5. Once patients had received the higher dose without experiencing an AE that met the definition of a DLT or required post-administration hospitalization, they were eligible for further escalations.

sec.title: Assessments
sec.p: All AEs, regardless of their relationship to study treatment, were reported and graded according to NCI CTCAE v5.0 (except for CRS which was assessed using the ASTCT grading scale21), and from initiation of study treatment until 2 months after the last dose of study treatment or until the initiation of a post study anti-cancer treatment, whichever occurred first.

Pharmacodynamic assessments were carried out in whole blood samples, CSF samples, and fresh or archival tumor biopsies to assess the proposed mechanism of action. IHC assays were used to assess CD8, FOXP3, and GZMB as well as CD68 and CD163 in solid tumor samples; details are provided in the Supplementary Methods. Pharmacokinetic analyses were carried out on serum and CSF samples (collected at baseline and cycle 2 day 3 or 8) using an enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay. Validated assays were used to detect anti-drug antibodies (ADAs) against EGFRvIII × CD3 TCB.

Response to treatment was assessed according to the Response Assessment in Neuro-oncology (RANO) criteria22 based on clinical and magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) evidence collected before and every 6 weeks after the start of study treatment in the first 6 months and then every 9 weeks. Measurable disease was defined as contrast-enhancing lesions with clearly defined margins by MRI scan, with two perpendicular diameters of at least 10 mm. Non-measurable disease was defined as either other enhancing measurable lesions, masses with margins not clearly defined (non-enhancing FLAIR/T2 lesions), or enhancing lesions with maximal perpendicular diameters less than the minimum size for measurability.

sec.title: Statistical Analysis
sec.p: No formal sample size calculation was conducted for this dose escalation study. Instead, the number of patients enrolled was determined by the observed DLTs and the number of cohorts required to identify the MTD. This adaptive approach allowed for flexibility in responding to patient outcomes and ensured patient safety. The MTD was defined as the dose that maximized the probability of an acceptable DLT rate (within the range of 20% to 33%) while ensuring that the probability of overdosing, defined as a DLT rate exceeding 33%, was less than 25%. All patients who received at least one dose of EGFRvIII × CD3 TCB were included in the safety analysis population, which was regarded as the default analysis set. Patients in the safety population were evaluable for PK if they had data from at least one postdose sample, and were evaluable for response if they had measurable disease at baseline and at least one response assessment per RANO before and after the start of study treatment. All safety-related analyses were performed using descriptive statistics. Progression-free survival (PFS) and overall survival were measured from the first study treatment and analyzed using the Kaplan–Meier method. Statistical analyses were performed using R version 4.0.3 (R Foundation for Statistical Computing, Vienna, Austria) and SAS version 9.4. PK parameters for EGFRvIII × CD3 TCB were determined via non-compartmental analysis.

sec.title: Accrual and Patient Demographics
sec.p: A total of 153 patients were pre-screened or screened at 12 sites in Australia, Europe (Spain, Denmark, Netherlands, Germany), USA and Canada between April 2022 and January 2024. Thirty-six eligible patients were enrolled in one of the 10 study cohorts (Supplementary Figure S2). In the first 8 cohorts, 29 patients received flat doses of EGFRvIII × CD3 TCB ranging from 0.004 to 6.5 mg Q3W. Cohorts 9 and 10 used a step-up schedule of 2.5/4 mg and 3/10 mg, respectively.

Most patients were men (64%), younger than 65 years (83%; median age: 53 years), and had a KPS of 90–100 (89%) (Table 1). The MGMT gene promoter was unmethylated in 32 patients (89%) and methylated in 4 patients (11%).

fn.p: aFor the Karnofsky Performance Status, the values obtained at screening are shown.

sec.title: Exposure to Study Drug
sec.p: All 36 patients received at least one dose of EGFRvIII × CD3 TCB. The median treatment duration was 4.9 months (range, 0–26), the median number of treatment cycles was 8 (range, 1–38). Eighteen of the 36 patients received an initial flat dose below the predicted pharmacological minimally active dose (mPAD) of approximately 0.4 mg Q3W. The protocol allowed intra-patient dose escalation, and at the data cutoff, for 24 patients the dose was escalated at least once, 24 patients had received at least one dose above the mPAD, and 8 patients had received at least one dose of the maximum tested dose of 10 mg.

At the data cutoff, 32 (89%) patients had discontinued study treatment, 30 of them due to progressive disease, and one each due to an AE (grade 3 seizure) and withdrawal of consent, while four patients were still on study treatment (10 mg Q3W) (Supplementary Figure S2).

sec.title: Safety
sec.p: Overall, EGFRvIII × CD3 TCB was well tolerated up to the highest tested dose of 10 mg Q3W. Most AEs were of grade 1 or 2 severity. Ten patients (28%) had at least one AE of grade 3 severity, and 5 (14%) had at least one treatment-related AE of grade 3 severity, which included seizure in two patients, and brain oedema, decreased lymphocyte count, and decreased neutrophil count in one patient each. One patient in the 2.2 mg flat dose cohort had a grade 4 AE (epilepsy). No fatal (grade 5) AEs were reported.

Of the 36 patients treated, 35 (97%) experienced AEs and 10 (28%) experienced serious AEs (SAEs). Four patients (11%) had SAEs that were considered related to EGFRvIII × CD3 TCB, including brain oedema in one patient in the 0.09 mg flat dose cohort, seizure in one patient each in the 0.75 mg flat dose and 2.5/4 mg SUD cohorts, and CRS in one patient in the 6.5 mg flat dose cohort (see Case Report below).

The SAE of seizure in the 2.5/4 mg SUD cohort occurred one day after the initial 2.5 mg EGFRvIII × CD3 TCB dose and was considered a DLT. No other DLTs were reported; thus, no MTD could be determined in this study.

The DLT reported as grade 3 seizure was the only AE that led to treatment discontinuation. Six patients (17%) experienced at least one AE that led to EGFRvIII × CD3 TCB dose modification or interruption. One patient in the 0.09 mg flat dose cohort had two related SAEs of brain oedema; the first event, which occurred 4 days after the second EGFRvIII × CD3 TCB dose of 0.09 mg, led to a dose reduction, and the second event occurred at the reduced dose of 0.03 mg and led to treatment discontinuation 7 weeks later. Five other patients experienced AEs leading to dose interruption (epilepsy and respiratory tract infection in one patient [6.5 mg], and neutrophil count decrease [0.01 mg], herpes zoster [0.03 mg], dysarthria [0.25 mg], and sepsis [0.75 mg] in one patient each); all were considered not related to EGFRvIII × CD3 TCB.

Figure 1 presents the most common AEs (any causality and EGFRvIII × CD3 TCB-related). Twenty-one patients (58%) had at least one treatment-related AE, the most common of which was headache in 8 patients (22%), followed by diarrhoea, fatigue, decreased lymphocyte count, decreased neutrophil count, pyrexia, and seizure in three patients each (8%). Less common treatment-related AEs included CRS in two patients (3%) and infusion-related reaction (IRR) in one patient. One patient experienced grade 1 CRS with fever during the initial 2.2 mg EGFRvIII × CD3 TCB infusion, and another patient experienced grade 2 CRS 3 days after the initial 6.5 mg EGFRvIII × CD3 TCB dose (for details, see Case Report below). One patient in the 3/10 mg SUD cohort experienced chills of grade 1 severity, indicative of an IRR, shortly after the fourth 10 mg dose. Of note, the antihistamine premedication previously administered to this patient had been electively withheld before this dose. All three patients who experienced an AE of CRS or IRR continued study treatment without dose modification.

caption.p: Tornado plot of the most common AEs (AEs that were considered related in ≥ 1 patient).

sec.title: Pharmacokinetics and Immunogenicity
sec.p: The PK of EGFRvIII × CD3 TCB in serum was as predicted based on allometric scaling from hFcRn Tg32 mice and was conducive to 3-weekly dosing due to its half-life of 10 days and high potency. The highest dose studied (10 mg) was still approximately 6-fold below the predicted active therapeutic range of 8.8 to 20 μg/mL with regards to the Cmax. A preliminary linear 2-compartment population PK model was built, and PK parameters are presented in Supplementary Table S1. The concentration of EGFRvIII × CD3 TCB increased proportionally with dose in both serum and CSF (Figure 2A). The CSF/serum ratio, based on the ratio of the slope of the regression lines, was 0.08, which was 10-fold lower than predicted based on preclinical results in rats.

caption.p: EGFRvIII × CD3 TCB pharmacokinetics and EGFRvIII staining intensity.

(A) Linear regression analysis of EGFRvIII × CD3 TCB concentrations in serum and CSF for the tested dose range. (B) Distribution of EGFRvIII staining intensity. Representative examples for low, medium, and high EGFRvIII staining intensity are shown in Supplementary Figure S3.

sec.p: Analysis of albumin quotient (QAlb) as an indicator of the blood-brain barrier (BBB) permeability indicated that at baseline, 34 patients had either no or a moderate disruption of the BBB, and two patients had a high BBB disruption, based on the criteria by Schmid et al.23 (Supplementary Table S2). No major changes in BBB disruption were observed on-treatment.

Six patients had detectable ADA titers, but only four of them (11% of all patients) were classified as ADA-positive, as they either had no ADA prior to treatment of EGFRvIII × CD3 TCB (0.25 mg flat dose [n = 1]) or 4 mg SUD [n = 2]), or an increase of more than 2-fold from the baseline titer (0.09 mg flat dose [n = 1]). No obvious relationship with dose and no discernible ADA effect on PK or safety was observed.

sec.title: Clinical Outcomes
sec.p: Of the 36 patients treated, 28 were response-evaluable (8 had no measurable disease at baseline); of these, the MGMT promoter status was unmethylated in 26 patients and methylated in two patients. No radiographic responses were observed. Six of the 26 patients (23%) with unmethylated MGMT had progressive disease, and 20 patients (77%) had stable disease as best confirmed overall response based on the response assessment according to RANO criteria (Figure 3A). Five of these patients had stable disease for ≥ 6 months after start of study treatment, of whom three patients received doses ≥ 6.5 mg dose cohorts (one patient after a gradual intra-patient dose escalation starting from an initial 0.004 mg dose).

caption.p: Clinical outcomes following treatment with EGFRvIII × CD3 TCB. (A) Swimlane plot for exposure to EGFRvIII × CD3 TCB and response over time based on RANO criteria for all 36 enrolled patients. (B) Kaplan-Meier estimate of progression-free survival for the 32 patients with an unmethylated MGMT promoter.

sec.p: The median follow-up time after the start of treatment, calculated using the reverse Kaplan–Meier method, was approximately 13.7 months. The median overall survival was not reached in the 32 patients with an unmethylated MGMT promoter. These patients had an mPFS of 4.4 months (95% CI: 3.7, 5.6) (Figure 3B) and a 1-year survival rate of 73% (95% CI: 54.4, 91.8). A subgroup consisting of 13 patients with an unmethylated MGMT promoter who received a dose of ≥ 6.5 mg for at least 2 cycles during the study had a median PFS of 5.1 months (95% CI: 2.6, not evaluable) and a 1-year survival rate of 91% (95% CI: 73.9, 100).

Two of the four patients with a methylated MGMT promoter were response-evaluable, one had durable stable disease (2.5/4 mg SUD cohort), while the other (2.2 mg flat dose cohort) had a PFS of 86 days. Of the other two patients, one was withdrawn due to a DLT (see safety section), and the other patient was still on-treatment (approximately 9 months after initiation) at the data cutoff.

sec.title: Pharmacodynamic/Biomarker Results
sec.p: Screening for EGFRvIII positivity (only EGFRvIII-positive patients were enrolled) through central laboratory EGFRvIII investigational IHC testing identified 44 positive cases (22 patients were pre-tested positive at a local laboratory [with varying methods] and confirmed positive at the central CAP/CLIA laboratory thereafter) of 103 cases tested in total (Figure 2B). Excluding the locally identified cases, the overall prevalence was 27% (≥ 1% tumor cell expression at ≥ 1 + intensity staining), which is consistent with the range of EGFRvIII positivity previously reported.13,24–28 The median histoscore (H-score) was 190 across the tested patient samples. No consistent relationship between administered dose and either peripheral pharmacodynamic changes (CD8 T cell margination) or cytokine release were observed in patients treated with up to 10 mg EGFRvIII × CD3 TCB.

Analysis of baseline and on-treatment (on-progression) biopsies from two patients enrolled in the 0.01 mg flat dose cohort showed no loss of target expression, and the on-treatment EGFRvIII levels and H-scores were in the range of the baseline values (Supplementary Figure S4A; Supplementary Table S3). Baseline tumor CD8 densities, which were low as expected for GBM (desert phenotype), increased upon treatment in these two patients, whereas there was no trend for FoxP3 and granzyme B changes (Supplementary Figure S4BandS4C). M2 macrophages covered a larger area than M1 macrophages in both patients pre- and on-treatment and increased further on-treatment in one patient (2% at baseline versus 34% on-treatment), (Supplementary Figure S4C). Triplex IHC analysis showed an increase in overall immune cells on-treatment (Supplementary Figure S4D). However, there was no increase in CD8 + GZMB + T cells as an indication of target engagement.

sec.title: Case Report
sec.p: A 53-year-old patient initially presented with ataxia and right-sided neglect. MRI was suspicious of left occipital-parietal GBM, and the patient underwent gross total resection. Histology confirmed the diagnosis of GBM with IDH wildtype WHO grade 4 and unmethylated MGMT promoter (5%). The patient received adjuvant radiation (60 Gy/30 fx) and concomitant temozolomide. At screening following completion of radiotherapy, the patient did not have measurable enhancing disease, but MRI revealed significant residual non-enhancing disease (splenium of the corpus callosum, 13 × 10 mm, posterior aspect of the left cingulate gyrus, 9 × 8 mm, Figure 4A). Central IHC showed an H-score of 220 for EGFRvIII tumor cell expression. The patient was neurologically intact at baseline.

caption.p: Characterization of the patient with tumor flare. (A) Magnetic resonance imaging and (B) measurements of peripheral blood CD 8 T cells (upper panel) and cytokines (lower panels) in this patient. C, cycle; D, day. (C) Serum EGFRvIII × CD3 TCB concentration data from this (yellow) and the other three patients included in the 6.5 mg cohort.

sec.p: The patient received the first dose of 6.5 mg EGFRvIII × CD3 TCB per protocol (day 1 of cycle 1 [C1D1]) following premedication with a corticosteroid, analgesic, and antihistamine. The patient presented with a low-grade headache on C1D2, which initially responded well to NSAID treatment. However, on C1D3, the patient developed a grade 3 headache, along with low-grade nausea, ataxia, confusion, and expressive dysphasia. Brain MRI revealed an increase in T2/FLAIR (Figure 4A) compared with the baseline assessment 11 days earlier. The headache improved with dexamethasone treatment. On C1D4, the patient experienced a grade 2 CRS event with persistent fever (> 38.5 °C), nausea, hypoxia, and chills as symptoms, while already receiving dexamethasone 10 mg IV Q6H for the cerebral edema and associated neurological symptoms. The fever and hypoxia resolved promptly after a single IV dose of 800 mg of tocilizumab. On C1D6, all symptoms were resolved except for persistent ataxia (grade 1). Peripheral blood cytokines, including IL-6 and IFN-γ, peaked on C1D3 (Figure 4B), consistent with the clinical observations. In addition, CD8 + T cell margination (−67.9%) was observed on C1D8, which is in line with the anticipated mode of action of this TCB. Serum EGFRvIII × CD3 TCB concentrations in this patient (yellow dots in Figure 4C) were as predicted and similar to those of the other patients in the 6.5 mg flat dose cohort; no ADA were detected in this cohort. Taken together, this event was interpreted as tumor flare related to treatment with EGFRvIII × CD3 TCB. The patient received two further doses of 6.5 mg EGFRvIII × CD3 TCB as per protocol, which were well tolerated. He discontinued 3 weeks after cycle 3 due to progressive disease.

sec.title: Discussion
sec.p: In this first-in-human dose escalation study, we explored the use of EGFRvIII × CD3 TCB in patients with newly diagnosed EGFRvIII-positive GBM. Overall, EGFRvIII × CD3 TCB was well tolerated up to the highest dose (10 mg Q3W) tested in this study. One DLT (grade 3 seizure) occurred in a patient following the initial 2.5 mg dose in the 2.5/4 mg SUD cohort. As no other DLTs were reported, the MTD was not reached. Four of the 36 treated patients (11%) were positive for anti-EGFRvIII × CD3 TCB ADAs, but their titers tended to decrease with continued treatment, and no obvious relationship with dose and no effect on PK was seen. The sponsor decided to discontinue the study before further dose escalation.

The majority of reported AEs were grade 1-2 neurotoxicities typically encountered in this disease setting.29 These events were pronounced in patients with significant residual disease following initial tumor resection and may have been indicative of mass effects induced through residual tumor inflammation. While a number of patients experienced on-treatment seizures and epileptic episodes, in most cases, pre-study seizures were reported in the medical history and may have also been associated with poor compliance with anti-seizure medications, emphasizing the importance of robust seizure prophylaxis when exploring an immunotherapy for GBM. Flat-dosing was used up to an EGFRvIII × CD3 TCB dose of 6.5 mg. However, a step-up dosing schedule, as used for other T cell-engaging therapies,30 was introduced as a precautionary measure, after a patient experienced tumor flare and grade 2 CRS at this dose level. CRS, a common concern of T cell-engaging therapies,31 occurred in 2 (6%) of the 36 patients (one grade 1 and one grade 2 event) in this study. CRS was therefore considerably less frequent than with bispecific antibodies in other solid tumors, such as small-cell lung cancer (approximately 50%)32 and metastatic uveal melanoma (up to 90%).33 The grade 2 CRS event was associated with an increase in T2/FLAIR signal on MRI as well as a peak in peripheral blood cytokines and rapid re-distribution of T cells from the periphery followed by T cell activation. This pharmacodynamic effect has been seen for other T cell bispecific antibodies and CAR T cell therapies34 and, although its onset may be delayed after EGFRvIII × CD3 TCB administration due to the BBB and location of the tumor, it supports the mode-of-action of EGFRvIII × CD3 TCB.

EGFRvIII × CD3 TCB concentrations showed a dose-proportional increase both in serum and CSF, with a CSF/serum ratio of 0.08, which is in line with the uptake of circulating antibodies into the brain.35 QAlb data indicated no or a moderate disruption of the BBB in 34 patients at baseline and a high disruption in two patients; no relevant changes were observed after the start of treatment. Serum concentrations at steady state immediately after administration of 10 mg Q3W remained 6-fold below the lower boundary of the predicted ATD, although pharmacodynamic effects in individual patients may already be evident at lower doses, as indicated by the described Case Report.

Our study primarily enrolled newly diagnosed GBM patients whose tumors harboured an unmethylated MGMT promoter. Patients with MGMT unmethylated tumors achieve nominal benefit from temozolomide maintenance therapy, with an mPFS of approximately 5 months from the start of chemoradiation.5,6 Enrollment of these patients after completion of standard radiation therapy allowed the evaluation of the safety profile of EGFRvIII × CD3 TCB in the adjuvant setting, shortly after EGFRvIII expression was confirmed. Disease symptoms are therefore less likely to have a confounding effect during this period, before EGFRvIII expression may be lost during disease recurrence.25 In our study, the median PFS was approximately 7 months from the start of radiotherapy in the 32 patients with an unmethylated MGMT promoter. None of the 26 response-evaluable patients with an unmethylated MGMT promoter had an objective response, but 5 (29%) had stable disease for ≥ 6 months. Although the median PFS observed in our study and the demonstration of durable disease control noted in a subset of patients are encouraging, conclusions regarding efficacy are not appropriate given the phase 1 nature of this study, coupled with the fact that the highest dose tested in this study was below the predicted ATD.
